results.claim: The literal simultaneous pyramid problem is an interval-permutation problem. Put m=ell+1 and a_i=min(r+i-1,n). If pos(i) is one plus the final row size occupied by colour i, then solutions are exactly permutations satisfying a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1, clipped to [1,n]. Thus the answer is the permanent of this interval matrix.
results.proof_sketch: The final multiplicities, including zero for the omitted colour, are 0,1,...,n-1. Hence assigning final multiplicities to the n labelled colours is equivalent to a permutation pos of [n]. Colour i has a_i-(pos(i)-1) objects removed. Requiring this number to lie in [0,m] gives exactly a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1. Conversely, any such permutation specifies a valid removal solution, so the correspondence is bijective.

results.claim: Let A_{n,ell,r} denote the answer, with 0<=r<=n and m=ell+1. Then A_{n,ell,0}=1; if r>=1 and m<r, then A_{n,ell,r}=0; and if r>=1, m>=r, and n<m, then A_{n,ell,r}=r!(r+1)^(n-r). For n>=m there is an explicit finite-state formula given below.
results.proof_sketch: For r=0, the initial multiplicities already are 0,1,...,n-1, so no removal is possible or necessary. If m<r, whichever colour receives final multiplicity zero must lose at least r objects, which violates the cap. If n<m, every initial multiplicity is at most n<m, so the limitation is inactive; the source's proved relaxed enumeration gives the flatorial r!(r+1)^(n-r).

results.claim: Assume 1<=r<=m<=n and set q=m-r. Let U={1-r,...,q}, let S be the q-subsets of U, and I={1,...,q}. Define T_{S,S'} as the number of x in S union {q+1} such that S'={y-1: y in (S union {q+1}) minus {x}} is a q-subset of U. For S={s_1<...<s_q}, put w(S)=r! product_{j=1}^q(s_j+r-j+1). Then A_{n,ell,r}=e_I^T T^(n-m) w.
results.proof_sketch: The colours 1,...,n-r have uncapped initial sizes r+i-1 and allowed positions i-q through i+r. The final r colours all have initial size n and are allowed only in the last m positions. Put K=n-m. During the first K positions only ordinary colours occur. After k positions, record the q introduced but unused ordinary colours by their offsets from k; these offsets form a q-subset S of U. The next ordinary colour has offset q+1. Choosing x for position k+1 and decrementing all remaining offsets gives precisely the stated transition; requiring the new state to lie in U enforces every right deadline. After K transitions, an ordinary colour with offset s has relative deadline s+r among the last m positions. If s_1<...<s_q, assigning these q distinct colours in deadline order gives product_j((s_j+r)-(j-1)) possibilities. The remaining r slots receive the r capped colours in r! orders, yielding w(S). Summing over terminal states proves the formula.

results.claim: For fixed ell and r with 1<=r<=m=ell+1, the complete ordinary generating function is rational: G_{ell,r}(z)=sum_{n>=r}A_{n,ell,r}z^n = r! sum_{n=r}^{m-1}(r+1)^(n-r)z^n + z^m e_I^T(I-zT)^(-1)w. Consequently A_{n,ell,r} satisfies an explicit constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most binomial(m,r) for n>=m.
results.proof_sketch: The finite sum covers the inactive-limit range. Expanding the inverse as sum_{k>=0}z^kT^k and applying the preceding transfer formula gives every term from n=m onward. The matrix has binomial(q+r,q)=binomial(m,r) states. If its characteristic polynomial is x^D+c_1x^(D-1)+...+c_D, Cayley-Hamilton gives A_{n+D}+c_1A_{n+D-1}+...+c_DA_n=0 for every n>=m.

results.claim: The physical simultaneous problem is generally not the naive intersection of the displacement bounds 'ell left' and 'r right.' For example, n=4, ell=1, r=2 has exactly two physical solutions, represented by 1234 and 1243, whereas the naive two-sided displacement class has seven permutations.
results.proof_sketch: Here m=2 and the initial multiplicities are 2,3,4,4. Direct application of the interval condition leaves only 1234 and 1243. For an uncapped colour i, the number removed is r+i-pos(i), so the physical cap gives i-pos(i)<=m-r=ell+1-r, not i-pos(i)<=ell. The final r colours also share one common terminal interval. Thus simply intersecting the two separately derived permutation descriptions changes the problem.

final_writeup:
Set m=ell+1, as in Section 3, and let A_{n,ell,r} count solutions obtained by applying that same per-colour removal cap to the relaxed initial pyramid of Section 7. Assume 0<=r<=n.

Colour i initially has

a_i=min(r+i-1,n)

objects. The target pyramid has multiplicities 1,...,n-1, together with multiplicity zero for the omitted colour. Write pos(i)=k when colour i receives final multiplicity k-1. The pos(i) form a permutation of [n], and the amount removed from colour i is

e_i=a_i-pos(i)+1.

Therefore the exact admissibility condition is

a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1,

with positions clipped to [1,n]. This already gives the permanent formula

A_{n,ell,r}=per( 1{max(1,a_i-m+1)<=k<=min(n,a_i+1)} )_{i,k=1}^n.

The following transfer formula makes the enumeration finite-state and supplies a rational generating function.

There are three immediate regimes. If r=0, then A_{n,ell,0}=1. If r>=1 but m<r, then A_{n,ell,r}=0, because some colour must be reduced to zero and every initial colour has at least r>m objects. If n<m, the limitation is inactive and the source's flatorial result gives

A_{n,ell,r}=r!(r+1)^(n-r).

It remains to treat 1<=r<=m<=n. Put

q=m-r,   U={1-r,2-r,...,q}.

Let the state set consist of all q-subsets S of U, and let I={1,...,q}; empty sets and empty products have their usual meanings when q=0. Define the integer transition matrix T by

T_{S,S'}=#{x in S union {q+1}: S'={y-1:y in (S union {q+1}) minus {x}} is contained in U}.

For S={s_1<...<s_q}, define

w(S)=r! product_{j=1}^q(s_j+r-j+1).

Then the exact answer is

A_{n,ell,r}=e_I^T T^(n-m) w,   n>=m.

To prove this, observe that colours 1,...,n-r have respective initial sizes r,...,n-1. Their permitted final positions are i-q,...,i+r. The remaining r colours all have size n and can occur only in positions n-m+1,...,n. Let K=n-m. During positions 1,...,K, only the first kind of colour can occur. After k such positions, exactly q introduced ordinary colours remain unused. Recording their labels relative to k produces a q-subset S of U. The next introduced colour has relative label q+1; choosing the colour placed next and decrementing every remaining relative label is exactly one transition of T. The lower endpoint 1-r enforces the right deadlines.

After K transitions, the last m positions remain. An ordinary colour with offset s has relative deadline s+r. If the remaining offsets are s_1<...<s_q, assign these colours in increasing deadline order. Colour j has s_j+r-(j-1) available slots, giving the displayed product. The r equal-sized terminal colours can then be assigned to the remaining slots in r! ways. This proves the transfer formula.

For fixed ell,r with 1<=r<=m, the full generating function is

G_{ell,r}(z)=sum_{n>=r}A_{n,ell,r}z^n
 = r! sum_{n=r}^{m-1}(r+1)^(n-r)z^n
   + z^m e_I^T(I-zT)^(-1)w.

It is rational. Since T has D=binomial(m,r) states, its characteristic polynomial gives a homogeneous constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most D for all n>=m. This completely enumerates the literal simultaneous pyramid problem, including all boundary cases.
